# Topics in Atomic Physics

## Integrals of Three Spherical Harmonics

## Alkali-Atom Energy Levels in an External Magnetic Field

## Fine Structure of S Electrons and the Darwin Term

$$
{E_{{\rm{SO}}}} = \frac{{j(j + 1) - l(l + 1) - {3 \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {3 4}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 4}}}{2}{\beta _{nl}}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2321}

where

$$
\;{\beta _{nl}} \equiv {\hbar ^2}\int_0^\infty {b\left( r \right)R_{n,l}^2\left( r \right){r^2}dr} \; = \frac{{{Z^4}{\alpha ^2}}}{{{n^3}l\left( {l + 1} \right)\left( {l + 1/2} \right)}}{E_{\rm{H}}}{\rm{,}} \qquad  \;\;\;\;l > 0
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2323}

Therefore

$$
\begin{array}{c} {E_{{\rm{SO}}}}(j) = \frac{{j(j + 1) - l(l + 1) - {3 \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {3 4}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 4}}}{2}{\beta _{nl}}\\ = \left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{,\;l = 0}\\ {\left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\frac{l}{2}{\beta _{nl}},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;j = l + \frac{1}{2}}\\ { - \frac{{l + 1}}{2}{\beta _{nl}},\;\;j = l - \frac{1}{2}} \end{array}} \right.}&{,\;l > 0} \end{array}} \right. \end{array}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2325}

An interesting observation is that, although for $l=0$ the first factor of ${E_{{\rm{SO}}}}$ vanishes and there is no spin–orbit coupling, and although ${\beta }_{nl}$ is meaningful only for $l>0$, formally evaluating the expression at $j=l+1/2$ while ignoring the condition $l>0$ allows $l$ to cancel between numerator and denominator, giving

$$
{E_{{\rm{SO}}}} = \frac{{{Z^2}{\alpha ^2}}}{n}\left\vert  {E_n^{(0)}} \right\vert \;, \qquad  {\rm{for}}\;l = 0,j = 1/2
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2327}

This equals the Darwin term for an $s$ electron.

## Fine and Hyperfine Structure of S Electrons

First consider the origin of the Fermi contact interaction in hyperfine structure.

Because the nucleus is much heavier than an electron, its spatial distribution can be approximated as a point relative to the electron cloud. With the nucleus at the origin, the probability density of an S electron at the nucleus is

$$
{\left\vert  {{\psi _{n,l = 0}}(0)} \right\vert ^2} = \frac{1}{\pi }{\left( {\frac{Z}{{n{a_0}}}} \right)^3}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2332}

The magnetization at the nucleus due to the electron's magnetic moment is

$$
{\bf{M}} = {{\bf{\mu }}_S}{\left\vert  {{\psi _{n,l = 0}}(r = 0)} \right\vert ^2}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2334}

Electrodynamics gives the magnetic field inside a uniformly magnetized sphere as

$$
{{\bf{B}}_{\rm{e}}} = \frac{2}{3}{\mu _0}{\bf{M}}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2336}

The potential energy of the nuclear magnetic moment in this magnetized electron cloud—the Fermi contact interaction—is therefore

$$
\begin{array}{c} {{\hat H}_{{\rm{NS}}}}(l = 0) = - {{{\bf{\hat \mu }}}_I} \cdot {{{\bf{\hat B}}}_{\rm{e}}} = {g_I}{\mu _{\rm{B}}}\frac{{{\bf{\hat I}}}}{\hbar } \cdot \left[ { - \frac{2}{3}{\mu _0}{g_S}{\mu _B}\frac{{{\bf{\hat S}}}}{\hbar }\frac{1}{\pi }{{\left( {\frac{Z}{{n{a_0}}}} \right)}^3}} \right]\\ = {g_I}\mu _{\rm{B}}^2\frac{{4{\mu _0}}}{{3\pi }}{\left( {\frac{Z}{{{a_0}n}}} \right)^3}\frac{{{\bf{\hat I}} \cdot {\bf{\hat S}}}}{{{\hbar ^2}}}\\ = \frac{{8{g_I}{Z^3}{\alpha ^2}}}{{3{n^3}}}{E_{\rm{H}}}\frac{{{\bf{\hat I}} \cdot {\bf{\hat S}}}}{{{\hbar ^2}}} \end{array}
$$ {#eq-zeqnnum480315}

Darwin term, the following analysis is wrong and it is missing a factor of Z. The Darwin term comes from Coulomb potential and has nothing to do with magnetic dipole interaction.

By analogy, replacing the nuclear magnetic moment ${{\bf{\hat \mu }}_I}$ in @eq-zeqnnum480315 with the electron moment ${{\bf{\hat \mu }}_S}$ would give the electron's potential energy in its own magnetic field:

$$
\begin{array}{c} {{\hat H}_{{\rm{SS}}}}(l = 0) = - {{{\bf{\hat \mu }}}_S} \cdot {{{\bf{\hat B}}}_{\rm{e}}} = - {{{\bf{\hat \mu }}}_S} \cdot \frac{2}{3}{\mu _0}{\bf{M}}\\ = - \frac{2}{3}{\mu _0}{\bf{\mu }}_S^2{\left\vert  {{\psi _{n,l = 0}}(r = 0)} \right\vert ^2} = - \frac{{8{g_S}{Z^3}{\alpha ^2}}}{{3{n^3}}}{E_{\rm{H}}}\frac{{{{{\bf{\hat S}}}^2}}}{{{\hbar ^2}}}\\ = - \frac{{4{Z^3}{\alpha ^2}}}{{{n^3}}}{E_{\rm{H}}} \end{array}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2341}

This calculation is not self-consistent: ${{\bf{\hat \mu }}_S}$ treats the electron as a point, whereas ${{\bf{\hat B}}_{\rm{e}}}$ treats it as a distribution. If it is treated consistently as a distribution, the self-energy of a uniformly magnetized sphere from electrodynamics is

$$
\begin{array}{c} {H_{SS}} = \frac{{{\mu _{0}}}}{6}{{\bf{M}}^2}V = \frac{2}{3}{\mu _0}{\bf{M}} \cdot \frac{1}{4}{\bf{M}}V = = \frac{2}{3}{\mu _0}{\bf{M}} \cdot \frac{{{{\bf{\mu }}_S}}}{4}\\ = \frac{{{Z^3}{\alpha ^2}}}{{{n^3}}}{E_{\rm{H}}} = \frac{{Z{\alpha ^2}}}{n}\left\vert  {E_n^{(0)}} \right\vert  \end{array}
$$ {#eq-ch10-p2343}

This result equals the Darwin term.
